issues.explanation: Occupation 'Retired' is implausible for age 28 (retired is implausible if age < 50).

issues.item: Memory: Verbal Access: I can talk about what happened very easily.
issues.explanation: Within Memory, 'I can talk about what happened very easily' sits awkwardly with 'my memories are very clear and detailed' and 'mostly pictures or images' for a PTSD profile tied to a life-threatening accident; this pattern suggests unusually easy verbal processing despite vivid intrusive-style memory, which weakens coherence of the memory node.

issues.item: Threat: Checking Behind: I frequently look behind me to check if someone is following me
issues.explanation: The threat item about repeatedly checking whether someone is following him implies an interpersonal pursuit/assault-type danger theme, which is hard to reconcile with the indexed trauma being a life-threatening accident and with the rest of the profile, which does not otherwise indicate persecution-related threat.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Other-Blame Rumination: I dwell on what other people have done to me
issues.explanation: 'I dwell on what other people have done to me' also implies an interpersonal harm/blame theme that does not fit well with the accident trauma context or the other selected appraisals, memories, and threats.

issues.item: Undereating: I avoid eating or restrict food as a way of coping
issues.explanation: Restricting food as a coping strategy is not well supported by the rest of the profile. The other items describe accident-related sensory threat (loud sounds, startle), image-based trauma memory, and self-critical appraisals, with maladaptive responses centered on avoidance/removal from reminders and rumination/meaning seeking. Undereating introduces a qualitatively different coping pattern that is not reflected elsewhere in Triggers, Threat, Memory, or Negative Appraisals, making it the least clinically coherent item in this five-component profile.

vignette: John, a 52-year-old European American film director, has been struggling with the aftermath of a life-threatening accident that occurred over six months ago. John was directing a scene for a movie on location in the wilderness when an unexpected landslide caused part of the set to collapse. The event left him pinned beneath debris and trapped until he could be rescued by the emergency response team. Since then, the experience has been hauntingly vivid in his mind. He recalls every detail with shocking clarity-the sound of earth crumbling, the panic that surged through him as he realized he was trapped, and the suffocating darkness around him. John's memories are mostly visual; flashes of debris raining down on him and the faces of frantic crew members emerge unbidden at unexpected moments. To cope with these intrusive thoughts, John has developed several maladaptive strategies. He often finds himself seeking answers to why this happened to him, spending hours ruminating on the event's meaning in his life. In an attempt to avoid triggers, he stays away from dark places and avoids revisiting locations that remind him of the accident site. This includes avoiding outdoor filming during dusk or night scenes. John's hypervigilance has become a constant presence in his daily routine. He is superalert at all times, always on guard for any unexpected sounds or movements that might bring back memories of the landslide. The sudden noise of a car honking outside or an abrupt clap from inside his home can send him into a state of intense anxiety. His startle response has become so exaggerated that he often finds himself jumping out of his skin at ordinary, harmless noises. The vividness and clarity of these memories have made it nearly impossible for John to articulate what happened in words. The traumatic event is locked within images, making conversations about the incident difficult and frustrating. He struggles to convey his experiences verbally, which has affected his ability to communicate effectively with his partner and colleagues. John's negative appraisals are deeply rooted in feelings of inadequacy and a sense that he is a poor coper. The person he has become feels unrecognizable to him-a shadow of the confident director he once was. His hypervigilance and avoidance behaviors have started to take a toll on his work, leading to delays and conflicts with crew members who find his newfound caution disruptive. His partner has noticed these changes and is concerned about their impact on their relationship. John's reluctance to discuss what happened openly has created a barrier between them, and he has become more isolated within the household. He avoids social gatherings that might expose him to loud noises or unfamiliar environments, further distancing himself from his loved ones. Despite his efforts to cope, John's symptoms have progressively worsened over time. The persistent avoidance and hypervigilance have led to a decline in his overall quality of life, affecting both his professional and personal relationships. What frightened him most was the realization that he might never fully regain control of his life or feel safe again. Finally, after months of struggling with these overwhelming feelings and behaviors, John has decided to seek help. He is hopeful that therapy can provide the tools he needs to manage his symptoms better and perhaps find a way to understand and process what happened without feeling so overwhelmed by it every day. The idea of regaining some sense of normalcy and reconnecting with those around him gives him hope, even as he acknowledges the challenges ahead.
